header.title: Software Development Engineer I, Java
header.lead: Your first engineering job, at a company small enough that what you write this week is live next week. You'll be taught, reviewed and stretched — and trusted with real work far earlier than most places would.
header.punchline: The floor is the same at every level here. What changes is how much of it you carry alone.

the_role.lead: We're hiring engineers at the start of their careers who we think will be very good in three years, and we're willing to invest to get there.
paragraphs: You'll join a team that owns a domain — claims, wallet, subscriptions, provider network or payments — and you'll take features inside it. Not toy tickets kept away from anything important. Real features, with a senior engineer reviewing your design before you build and your code before it ships.

Java and Spring Boot are where you'll spend most of your time. You'll also touch React screens and Node services, because features here don't stop at a language boundary. You're not expected to know all of it on day one. You are expected to learn it faster than is comfortable.

You'll be given context rather than instructions: why the feature exists, who it's for, what happens if it's wrong. Insurance is a domain with real rules, and a member may be relying on your screen during a hospital visit. Understanding that is part of the job, not background noise.

The deal is simple. We'll teach you, review you honestly, and let you near things that matter early. In return we expect you to ask a lot of questions, take feedback without flinching, and get measurably better every month.

the_level.lead: You're not expected to arrive knowing the answers. These six are what the level does ask for.

rows.text: A feature, or a well-defined piece of one. Someone helps you shape it.
The problem arrives mostly specified. You notice the parts that aren't, and ask.
Your own work, and the quality of every file you touch on the way past.
Knowing what you can decide and what you should ask about. Both are skills.
You test what you write, you don't break the build, and you say so the moment you do.
You need less help this month than last month. That's the whole job.

groups.label: DESIGN
bullets: Write the **LLD** for what you build — the schema, the API contract, the states a record can be in — and walk someone senior through it before you write the code.
Sit in the **HLD** discussions for your domain and follow them properly. Ask when you lose the thread; at this level not following is a bigger problem than not knowing.
Say out loud what you think the failure cases are. Being wrong about them in a review costs nothing. Missing them in production costs a member.

groups.label: BUILD
bullets: Write Java services and React screens for a domain you're still learning, against a design you've walked through with someone senior first.
Turn a ticket into working, tested code — and say early when the ticket itself is wrong. Spotting that is worth more than finishing it quietly.
Write the tests as you go. Not as a follow-up ticket, and not because someone asked.
Read a great deal more code than you write for the first few months. That's the fastest way in.

groups.label: RUN
bullets: Stay with what you shipped. Check the dashboard after a release rather than moving straight to the next thing.
Debug your own bugs first — logs, then the code, then a person. Come with what you already ruled out.
Shadow the on-call rotation before you join it, so the first real incident isn't your first look at the tooling.
Treat member data as confidential by default. Health and money information isn't something you get a second chance with.

groups.label: GROW
bullets: Take code review as the fastest free teaching you'll ever get. Argue when you disagree; change your mind when you're wrong.
Ask early and in the open. A blocked afternoon is expensive; a question costs nothing.
Learn the domain, not only the syntax — what a claim is, why a wallet balance moves, what a regulator requires.
Aim to be the person someone else asks by the end of your first year.

the_bar.intro: We'll teach you the technical parts. These five aren't things we can teach, so we select for them.

traits.title: High ownership
traits.text: Your feature is yours until it's live and working, not until the pull request is merged. If it breaks the next week, you want to be the one who finds out first.

traits.title: Highly motivated and self-driven
traits.text: You look for the next useful thing rather than waiting to be assigned it, and you say clearly and early when something is going to slip.

traits.title: Extensive AI use
traits.text: You already use Copilot, Claude or ChatGPT daily — and you can still explain every line you ship, because the point is to learn faster, not to skip learning.

traits.title: Fast, with a floor under it
traits.text: You ship in days, not weeks, and you don't buy that speed by skipping tests or leaving a mess behind you.

traits.title: Direct and low-ego
traits.text: You say "I don't know" quickly, you ask the question you're slightly embarrassed to ask, and you take a hard code review as help rather than as criticism.

ai.lead: AI-assisted development is the default here, not a novelty. For someone early in their career it's a genuine accelerant — and the easiest way to stall.
bullets: Use Copilot, Claude or ChatGPT every day — scaffolding, tests, refactors, debugging, understanding an unfamiliar codebase.
Read and own every line you ship. "The AI wrote it" is not an explanation for a production incident.
**If you can't explain it in review, don't ship it.** This is the one we'll hold you to hardest at this level.
Use it to learn faster, not to skip learning. Ask it *why*, make it show you the alternative, then decide for yourself.
Be careful where it's weakest — our domain rules, security-sensitive paths, and anything touching money or member health data. Verify those yourself.

minimum.note: Kafka, monitoring and observability, and both altitudes of system design are floor requirements at every level here, including this one. What differs at SDE I is the depth we expect, not whether you have it at all.
items: **0–2 years** of professional experience, internships included. New graduates are welcome and expected.
**Solid Java** — you can write clean, correct code without the IDE doing the thinking for you.
**Data structures and algorithms** you genuinely understand, rather than patterns you've memorised.
**SQL** — you can write a join, and reason about why a query is slow.
**CS fundamentals** — OOP, the basics of concurrency, HTTP, and how a database and a network actually behave.
**LLD** — you can design the schema and the API contract for a small feature, and name its edge cases without being walked through them.
**HLD** — you can draw a system's components, say what calls what, and point at where it would break. A real attempt, not a finished architecture.
**Kafka** or a similar event-driven system — you've built with it, and you can explain what a partition, a consumer group and consumer lag actually are.
**Monitoring and observability** — you answer questions with dashboards, logs and traces rather than guesses, and you've added a metric or an alert yourself.
**Git**, and the habit of small, readable commits someone else can follow.
**Some Spring Boot** exposure, or clear evidence you get productive in a new framework quickly.
**Daily AI use** already part of how you work.
**Clear communication** — you can explain what you built, and say precisely what you're stuck on.
**Bachelor's degree** in Computer Science, Engineering or a related field, or equivalent practical evidence.
An internship, or a project where people other than you actually used what you built.
Anything you shipped end to end — small is fine, a side project is fine — that you can explain the trade-offs on.
React, or any modern frontend framework.
Node.js or TypeScript.
Competitive programming, open-source contributions, or a portfolio we can read.
You've built something with an LLM API, not only used AI tooling.
Exposure to cloud, Docker or CI — even at a hobby level.
Any exposure to healthcare, insurance or fintech.

toolkit.label: OUR STACK
toolkit.note: You won't know all of this on day one, and we don't expect you to. You should expect to have touched most of it by the end of your first year.

rows.value: React web, React Native mobile app
Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT — in the daily workflow

assessment.lead: Six dimensions. At this level we're reading fundamentals, design instinct and rate of learning — not the length of your CV.

cards.title: Coding and fundamentals
cards.text: Correct, readable code under time pressure, plus data structures, complexity and enough of how databases and networks behave to reason about a real system.

cards.title: Low-level design
cards.text: An API and a data model for a small feature. Clear contracts, sensible tables, and the edge cases you raise before we do.

cards.title: High-level design
cards.text: A small system sketched out loud — components, what calls what, where it breaks. We're reading instinct and questions, not a finished architecture.

cards.title: Debugging
cards.text: Something that doesn't work. What you check first, how you narrow it down, and whether you guess or verify.

cards.title: Project deep-dive
cards.text: Something you built. Why those choices, what you'd do differently, and how much of it you can still explain.

cards.title: Learning and collaboration
cards.text: How you handle a concept you haven't met, feedback you disagree with, and admitting you don't know.

items: You want months of structured training before touching anything real. You'll be in production code in your first weeks.
You expect design to be someone else's job until you're senior. You'll be asked for a schema and a failure mode in your first months, and in the interview before that.
You want to write code and never read anyone else's. Most of the learning here comes the other way round.
You'd rather stay quiet than say you're stuck. Silence is the one failure mode we can't work with.
You want to specialise immediately. The first year is deliberately broad — backend, a bit of frontend, some infrastructure.
You're uncomfortable working where a bug can delay someone's hospital admission. That's the seriousness this team runs at.
